transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-03
Time: 15:00 EST
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Nguyen (Redwood SE), Sanaa Iqbal (Nebula Head of ML), Tom Reynolds (Nebula Infra), Priya Shah (Nebula CTO)
Links shared: https://redwood.ai/docs/catalog-playbook.pdf, benchmark-sheet (Google Sheet link), security-pack (redwood-security.pdf)

Summary:
Quick walkthrough of Redwood model catalog scouting playbook: how we pick open models, read benchmark signals, interpret kernel/hardware compatibility matrices, and move from shortlist to pilot. Discussed dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs and KMS/SOC2 concerns. Agreed to pilot with 3 shortlisted models and run latency+cost benches next week.

Topics covered:
- Catalog filters and scoring heuristics
- Benchmark interpretation (throughput, p50/p95/p99, token cost)
- Kernel mapping and quantization hints for different GPU families
- Routing policies: region vs cost vs latency
- Security: KMS, audit logs, private deployment options

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. I think it's about 45 minutes, we want to show our scouting playbook — how teams go from a wide open-model list to three candidates for a pilot, and then the bench plan. Liam's going to drive the catalog demo, I'll jump in on pricing/pilot structure and next steps.
[00:18] Sanaa (Nebula): Awesome, thanks. Quick context — we run a customer-facing summarization service, about 1200 qps peak, but bursty, and our current p99 is around 420ms on CPU hosts. We're exploring offloading to GPU inference to cut token cost and improve tail latency. Main asks: 1) model quality parity with our baseline, 2) p99 < 200ms ideally, and 3) encryption and audit controls.
[00:45] Maya: Great. That's helpful. Tom, is your infra team okay with a hosted flow first, or are you leaning private/VPC from day one?
[00:58] Tom: We prefer hosted for speed, but any customer data that touches the model needs to be encrypted and we need audit logs. If hosted can't provide the KMS/HSM integration we might need private.
[01:10] Liam (Redwood): Quick note — Redwood Hosted supports customer-managed keys through our KMS integration and we can show audit logs in Console retention. For the pilot we usually do hosted with an option to migrate to dedicated or private if there's a compliance blocker.
[01:30] Priya: Okay good. Can you start with the catalog scouting demo? We want to see how you rank models for summarization workloads.
[01:38] Liam: Yup. Pulling up the catalog now, you'll see filters on task (summarization), sequence length, cost bracket, and latency profile. The playbook we use is: score by quality on domain prompts, then weight by latency/cost based on your SLOs.
[02:05] [screen share noises] Liam: Here we have a shortlist — three open variants that commonly show up: an LLM-variant-7B-quant, a 13B opt-quant, and a trimmed instruction-tuned 3B. The catalog shows baseline benches we run on A100 and H100, and a compatibility matrix for kernels (cuda kernels, triton fallback, and our optimized fused-attn for certain models).
[02:40] Sanaa: I see a lot of numbers, how should we read p95 vs p99 across GPUs?
[02:48] Liam: Good question. The p95 is often where batching pays off; p99 shows tail effects — KV cache size, memory pressure, and sequence length variance affect p99. In the catalog we annotate benches with sample sequence-length distributions so you can map your traffic. For your 1200 qps bursty profile we recommend looking at p99 on H100-like configs or Redwood Dedicated pools with burst capacity.
[03:20] Tom: There's a column called kernel_map, what's that? 
[03:24] Liam: That's our kernel mapping hint — it suggests the best execution path. For example, some models benefit from our fused attention kernel on H100; others fall back to Triton kernels. The mapping indicates which kernels we pick and whether quantization to int8 or q4/x4 is safe.
[03:45] Sanaa: How reliable are the quantization recommendations? We worry about quality regressions.
[03:52] Liam: We produce delta-quality hooks. For each model we include small eval suites — per-prompt metrics that show relative BLEU/ROUGE or embedding similarity vs FP16 baseline. We flag models where q4 causes >X% drop in your metric. It's not perfect; we recommend running the model on a small in-house eval set in the pilot.
[04:20] Priya: Can you show an example bench?
[04:25] Liam: Sure. Opening the detailed bench for the 13B opt-quant. You'll see columns: seq_len, tokens/sec, p50, p95, p99, tokens_cost_usd, memory_peak. There's also a kernel column that lists 'fused-attn-v2' for H100 and 'triton-opt' for A100. In our notes we call out that at seq_len=512 the fused-attn path drops p99 by ~120ms vs triton for the same batch config.
[04:58] Sanaa: So for our p99 goal of <200ms — sounds like H100 + fused-attn and dedicated pool is safest. But cost is a factor.
[05:10] Maya: Exactly. The Optimize toolkit helps: we can simulate cost/latency tradeoffs by sweeping quantization and batch sizes. For example, q8+fused-attn gives similar quality and cuts token cost by ~30% compared to fp16 in that bench. We can include that scenario in the pilot.
[05:34] Tom: What about routing policies? We have global traffic and want cost-sensitive routing — route to cheaper variant for non-critical lanes.
[05:42] Liam: We support routing by label — route by latency SLO first, fallback to cheaper quantized variant if latency or capacity is not met. The Console shows you per-model routing rules and hit rates. We can also route by region or customer tier.
[05:58] Priya: Security — you mentioned KMS and audit logs earlier. Are keys managed by us?
[06:05] Maya: We integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and HSM partners). Hosted can be configured to use customer-managed keys for payload encryption at rest and for optional in-flight envelope keys. Audit logs are pushed to your SIEM via secure forwarding; Console has an audit trail for API calls per token. For private deployment we give you full control of keys on-prem.
[06:36] Sanaa: Good. For model selection in the playbook, how do you account for domain-specific quality? We have finance/legal terminologies.
[06:45] Liam: We include model tag metadata: instruction-tuned vs base, presence of domain fine-tune, and size. More importantly, we allow you to attach your own eval set to the catalog — you upload a small labeled set and our Optimize will score models for you and produce a ranked shortlist. We also provide prompt templates and calibration suggestions to reduce hallucinations.
[07:10] Tom: Are the benchmark numbers reproducible in our env? We need to run p99 benches with our traffic pattern.
[07:16] Liam: Yes — that's the pilot. We'll run the Redwood bench runner in your account or on a dedicated host, replaying a sampled traffic trace. The bench runner outputs the same schema as the catalog benches, so you can directly compare.
[07:30] Sanaa: What's the typical pilot scope? 3 models, run latency and quality benches, two weeks?
[07:36] Maya: That's our standard: pick 3 candidates from the catalog, run bench + small eval set, compare p50/p95/p99 and quality deltas, and then pick one for a canary deployment. Timeline is usually 2–3 weeks for the bench and 1 week for a small canary.
[07:50] Priya: Any gotchas with quantized models in terms of runtime stability? We've seen OOMs when kv cache grows.
[07:58] Liam: Good point. We annotate cache behavior in the catalog; some quantized kernels reduce memory margin and you'd need to tune kv cache eviction or pin a larger instance. Our Dedicated pools can auto-scale to avoid OOMs, and we recommend spot-checking memory_peak for long sequences.
[08:18] Tom: About Dedicated — is burst capacity a separate pool or same? How do SLAs apply?
[08:25] Maya: Dedicated has reserved capacity and optional burst capacity that leverages extra clusters. SLA applies to the reserved baseline; burst is best-effort but we have configurable policies. For strict business flows we recommend a Reserved+Burst with auto-fallback to a smaller cheaper model if capacity is constrained.
[08:45] Sanaa: Can you quantify cost differences? Even rough numbers help prioritize.
[08:50] Liam: In the bench sheet we list tokens_cost_usd per 1M tokens across model+quant combos. Example: 13B fp16 on H100 might be $X per 1M tokens, q4 reduces that by ~35%, and a 3B instruction-tuned model can be 60% cheaper but quality delta might be material on complex summarization. We'll include a cost sim graph for your expected qps.
[09:15] [small cross talk] Tom: Are there prebuilt adapters for embeddings or reranking? We might use both.
[09:22] Liam: Yes — the catalog has model tags by capability. We also provide end-to-end flow: candidate selection for generation + reranker/embedding pairing to improve final quality.
[09:35] Sanaa: Okay, practical question: how do we attach our eval set to the catalog?
[09:40] Maya: We have a small uploader in Console under Optimize -> Eval. You upload CSV with reference outputs and Redwood runs a suite of comparison metrics. We then produce a ranked CSV plus a recommended quantization and kernel path.
[09:55] Priya: If we find a custom fine-tune performs best, can we bring that model into Redwood for serving?
[10:02] Liam: Yes, you can bring a model artifact. We support pinned model versions and private model storage. We recommend packaging the tokenizer and the converted artifacts with the model bundle; our onboarding ops team helps convert to optimal kernels. For private deployments we can accept a tarball or container.
[10:22] Sanaa: Any legal/procurement stuff to know up front?
[10:26] Maya: We'll send an SOW template and the security pack. For enterprise we do a standard DPA and support SSO/SAML, RBAC. That will be in the next steps.
[10:38] Tom: Great. Can we talk about the kernel mapping a bit deeper — e.g., how do you decide fused-attn vs triton?
[10:45] Liam: It's a combination of architecture heuristics and empirical tests. We map model operator patterns to kernels: some attention patterns fuse nicely, others have custom ops. We also consider sequence length distribution and batch sizes. Our kernel selector runs a small calibration run and picks the fastest stable kernel. In Console you can override kernel selection for a route.
[11:10] Sanaa: Do you expose the kernel logs so our infra team can audit runtime decisions?
[11:15] Liam: Yes. Console tracing includes kernel-level annotations and per-request routing traces. Those traces can be exported to your tracing system.
[11:28] Priya: One last thing — fallback policies. If the chosen variant exceeds latency we want an automatic fallback to a cheaper model that maintains functional correctness.
[11:36] Maya: We have rollout policies that define thresholds for p95/p99 or error rate. If thresholds are violated, Redwood can route to a pre-defined fallback model or to a degraded mode (e.g., reduce max tokens). You define those in the route.
[11:52] Sanaa: Sounds good. Let's recap and next steps.
[11:56] Maya: Recap — Redwood will: 1) send the catalog playbook PDF and benchmark sheet, 2) propose three candidate models based on your eval set and the catalog, 3) Liam will draft a bench plan to replay your traffic, and 4) we'll run a hosted pilot with customer KMS and audit logs enabled.
[12:20] Tom: Action items from our side — we'll share traffic profile and SLO doc, plus a small eval set (100–200 samples) for scoring.
[12:35] Maya: Great. I'll follow up with pricing and a pilot template.
[12:40] Sanaa: Thank you. One minor note — please include kernel memory margins in the bench output, we need that for capacity planning.
[12:48] Liam: Noted. We'll add memory_peak and kv_cache footprint to the exported bench CSV.
[12:55] Priya: Okay thanks, that was useful.
[13:00] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll send notes and a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff for week of 2026-08-10.

End of transcript.
